title: Convenience and comfort: Reasons reported for using drugs alone among clients of harm reduction sites in British Columbia, Canada

claims.statement: In clients of 27 harm reduction supply sites across British Columbia, Canada, surveyed in 2018 (414 people aged 19 or older who had used illicit drugs in the past 6 months, recruited by convenience at the sites), 314 (75.8%; editors' 95% CI 71.5% to 79.7%) said they had used drugs alone at least once in the past 7 days, and 198 (47.8%) more than a quarter of the time, answering one question that did not define alone (Papamihali et al., 2020). Offered a short list of reasons, with more than one allowed, the 314 most often chose that it is more convenient and comfortable to use at home (139, 44.3%; 52.7% of the 264 who gave a reason, editors' calculation), then not wanting others to know (44, 14.0%; more often under age 50 than at 50 or older, 16.9% against 5.3%), having no one to use with (37, 11.7%), that it is safer to be alone (30, 9.6%) and not wanting to share or it being cheaper (27, 8.6%); written answers included having no access to an overdose prevention site and not being allowed to use in a transition home. People who used alone more often had no regular housing (37.6% against 24.0% of those who did not use alone; adjusted odds ratio 2.27, 95% CI 1.20 to 4.27, in 306 people with complete answers) and more often had used crack or cocaine in the past week (41.4% against 26.0%; 2.10, 1.15 to 3.82). They also more often reported an overdose in the past 6 months (22.9% against 15.0%), but not significantly after adjustment (1.71, 0.79 to 3.69); both were reported by the same people at one sitting, so this is an association, not a prediction, and the survey cannot say whether using alone changes the risk of overdose. Coroners' reports cited in the paper's background, not data of this study, found that 69% of people who died of an overdose in British Columbia in 2016–2017 were using alone and that in 2019 more than half of illicit drug overdose deaths happened in a private residence; the paper does not say how these deaths were defined or how using alone was established. People already in contact with services were surveyed, so the figures may not hold for people who use drugs and do not attend these sites. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
claims.magnitude: Used alone in the past 7 days: 314 of 414 (75.8%; editors' Wilson 95% CI 71.5% to 79.7%); more than 25% of the time: 198 (47.8%). Reasons (of 314): convenience and comfort at home 139 (44.3%; 52.7% of 264 giving a reason, editors' calculation), not wanting others to know 44 (14.0%), no one to use with 37 (11.7% as printed; 11.8% by editors' calculation), safer alone 30 (9.6%), not wanting to share or cheaper 27 (8.6%), other 19 (6.1%), prefer not to say 31 (9.9%), no response 19 (6.1%). Adjusted odds ratios (n = 306): no regular housing 2.27 (1.20 to 4.27); crack or cocaine 2.10 (1.15 to 3.82); opioids 1.59 (0.87 to 2.88); crystal methamphetamine 1.58 (0.86 to 2.88); overdose in the past 6 months 1.71 (0.79 to 3.69). Naloxone kit: 67.8% of those who used alone against 66.0%. Coroners' figures cited in the background: 69% of overdose deaths in 2016–2017 involved using alone; in 2019, more than half of illicit drug overdose deaths in a private residence and 26.5% in another residence.
